blocks.body:
Euler noticed that $n^2 + n + 41$ is prime for $n = 0, 1, \dots, 39$. At $n = 40$ it equals $40^2 + 40 + 41 = 41^2$. Was that bad luck, or must every polynomial eventually produce a composite number? And if $P$ has integer coefficients, can $P(1) = 2$ and $P(3) = 5$? Both questions have short answers once you know the basic fact of this lesson: for a polynomial $P$ with integer coefficients, $a - b$ always divides $P(a) - P(b)$.

That fact, together with a few classical companions (the rational root test, Gauss's lemma and counting roots modulo a prime), drives most olympiad problems about such polynomials. We write $\mathbb Z[x]$ for the set of polynomials with integer coefficients and use divisibility and congruences from [[divisibility]] and [[congruences]].

blocks.title: The basic divisibility
blocks.body:
Start with powers. $a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)$ and $a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)$. In general

$$a^k - b^k = (a - b)(a^{k-1} + a^{k-2}b + \dots + ab^{k-2} + b^{k-1}),$$

as you can check by multiplying out: all the middle terms cancel in pairs. If both $a$ and $b$ are integers, the second factor is an integer, so $a - b \mid a^k - b^k$. A polynomial with integer coefficients is an integer combination of powers, so the divisibility passes to it.

blocks.title: Difference divisibility
blocks.body:
Let $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$. For all integers $a, b$,

$$a - b \mid P(a) - P(b).$$

Equivalently, if $a \equiv b \pmod m$, then $P(a) \equiv P(b) \pmod m$.

Write $P(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{d} c_k x^k$ with $c_k \in \mathbb Z$. Then

$$P(a) - P(b) = \sum_{k=1}^{d} c_k\,(a^k - b^k),$$

since the constant terms cancel. Each $a^k - b^k$ is a multiple of $a - b$ by the factorisation above, and each $c_k$ is an integer, so the sum is a multiple of $a - b$. For the congruence form: if $m \mid a - b$, then $m \mid P(a) - P(b)$.

blocks.title: Integer and rational roots
blocks.body:
Three consequences are used constantly.

1. $P(n) \bmod m$ depends only on $n \bmod m$. To understand $P$ modulo $m$, you only have to test $m$ residues.
2. An integer root $r$ of $P$ divides $P(0)$, because $r - 0 \mid P(r) - P(0) = -P(0)$.
3. If $P(r) = 0$, then $r - a \mid P(a)$ for every integer $a$. Knowing a few values of $P$ therefore restricts where its integer roots can be.

The same idea gives rational roots. Suppose $P(x) = c_d x^d + \dots + c_1 x + c_0 \in \mathbb Z[x]$ and $u/v$ is a root in lowest terms. Multiplying $P(u/v) = 0$ by $v^d$ gives

$$c_d u^d + c_{d-1}u^{d-1}v + \dots + c_1 u v^{d-1} + c_0 v^d = 0.$$

Every term except the last is a multiple of $u$, so $u \mid c_0 v^d$; since $\gcd(u, v) = 1$, $u \mid c_0$. Similarly every term except the first is a multiple of $v$, so $v \mid c_d$. This is the rational root theorem: rational roots have numerators dividing the constant term and denominators dividing the leading coefficient.

blocks.title: Content and primitive polynomial
blocks.body:
The content $c(P)$ of a nonzero $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ is the greatest common divisor of its coefficients. $P$ is primitive if $c(P) = 1$.

Every nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients can be written as a rational number times a primitive polynomial in $\mathbb Z[x]$.

blocks.title: Gauss's lemma
blocks.body: The product of two primitive polynomials is primitive. Consequently, if $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ is a product of two nonconstant polynomials with rational coefficients, then it is a product of two nonconstant polynomials in $\mathbb Z[x]$ of the same degrees.

Let $f = \sum a_i x^i$ and $g = \sum b_j x^j$ be primitive, and suppose some prime $p$ divides every coefficient of $fg$. Because $f$ and $g$ are primitive, there is a smallest index $i_0$ with $p \nmid a_{i_0}$ and a smallest index $j_0$ with $p \nmid b_{j_0}$. The coefficient of $x^{i_0 + j_0}$ in $fg$ is

$$\sum_{i + j = i_0 + j_0} a_i b_j.$$

In every term other than $a_{i_0}b_{j_0}$, either $i < i_0$, so $p \mid a_i$, or $j < j_0$, so $p \mid b_j$. So the coefficient is congruent to $a_{i_0}b_{j_0} \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$, a contradiction. Hence $fg$ is primitive.

For the second statement, suppose $P = FG$ with $F, G \in \mathbb Q[x]$ nonconstant. Write $F = \alpha f$ and $G = \beta g$ with $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb Q$ and $f, g \in \mathbb Z[x]$ primitive, and write $\alpha\beta = u/v$ in lowest terms with $v > 0$. Then $vP = u\,fg$. The content of the left side is $v\,c(P)$; the content of the right side is $|u|$, because $fg$ is primitive. So $v\,c(P) = |u|$, hence $v \mid u$, and $\gcd(u, v) = 1$ forces $v = 1$. Thus $P = (uf)\cdot g$ with both factors in $\mathbb Z[x]$.

blocks.title: Factorisation and roots modulo primes
blocks.body:
Gauss's lemma means that to show an integer polynomial cannot be factored over $\mathbb Q$, it is enough to rule out factorisations with integer coefficients. The most useful test of this kind is Eisenstein's criterion: if a prime $p$ divides every coefficient of $P$ except the leading one, and $p^2 \nmid P(0)$, then $P$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. For example $x^n - 2$ is irreducible for every $n \ge 1$. (The proof imitates the argument above: reduce a hypothetical integer factorisation modulo $p$.)

Modulo a prime, polynomials behave as over any field. If $p \nmid c_d$, the congruence $P(x) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ has at most $d$ solutions modulo $p$ (Lagrange's theorem): each root $r$ lets you split off a factor $x - r$, and a product is $0$ modulo a prime only if a factor is. Modulo a composite number this fails: $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ has the four solutions $1, 3, 5, 7$. Solutions modulo $p$ can often be lifted to solutions modulo $p^k$ by [[hensel]], and solutions modulo different primes combined by [[crt]].

The other direction asks which primes divide some value $P(n)$. For $P(n) = n^2 + 1$ these are $2$ and the primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, by [[quadratic-residues]]. For every nonconstant $P$ there are infinitely many such primes (the fourth example), and how they are distributed is described by Chebotarev's density theorem.

blocks.title: Iterating a polynomial
blocks.body: Iterating a polynomial gives another family of problems. Write $P^{(k)} = P\circ P\circ\dots\circ P$ ($k$ times); here the superscript means composition, not a derivative. An integer $t$ with $P^{(k)}(t) = t$ is a periodic point. The difference divisibility applied around an orbit $t \to P(t) \to P(P(t)) \to \dots$ is very restrictive, because consecutive differences must divide each other in a cycle. The outcome is the following theorem, which was IMO 2006 Problem 5. The problem is in the site's problem bank, so we leave the proof to you.

blocks.title: Integer periodic points
blocks.body:
Let $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ with $\deg P > 1$, and let $k \ge 1$. Then

$$\#\{t \in \mathbb Z : P^{(k)}(t) = t\} \le \deg P.$$

blocks.title: An extremal example
blocks.body: The bound can be attained. For $P(x) = (x - 1)^2$ we have $P(0) = 1$ and $P(1) = 0$, an orbit of length $2$. The equation $P(P(t)) = t$ reads $t^2(t - 2)^2 = t$, that is, $t\,(t - 1)(t^2 - 3t + 1) = 0$, whose integer solutions are exactly $0$ and $1$: two of them, equal to $\deg P$. The hypothesis $\deg P > 1$ is needed: $P(x) = -x$ satisfies $P(P(t)) = t$ for every integer $t$.
Is there a polynomial $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ with $P(1) = 2$ and $P(3) = 5$? Show also that if $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ and both $P(0)$ and $P(1)$ are odd, then $P$ has no integer root.
blocks.solution:
No such $P$ exists: $3 - 1 = 2$ would have to divide $P(3) - P(1) = 3$.

For the second part, every integer $n$ is congruent to $0$ or $1$ modulo $2$, so $P(n) \equiv P(0)$ or $P(n) \equiv P(1) \pmod 2$. Either way $P(n)$ is odd, hence $P(n) \ne 0$.

blocks.body: Find all rational roots of $P(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 2$ and factor $P$ over $\mathbb Z$.
blocks.solution:
By the rational root theorem a root $u/v$ in lowest terms has $u \mid 2$ and $v \mid 2$, so the candidates are $\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm\tfrac12$. Testing:

$$P(1) = -2,\quad P(-1) = -2 - 3 + 3 + 2 = 0,\quad P(2) = 16 - 12 - 6 + 2 = 0,\quad P(\tfrac12) = \tfrac14 - \tfrac34 - \tfrac32 + 2 = 0.$$

A cubic has at most three roots, so the rational roots are $-1$, $2$ and $\tfrac12$, and

$$2x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x - 2)(2x - 1).$$

(Expand $(x+1)(x-2) = x^2 - x - 2$ and multiply by $2x - 1$ to confirm.)

blocks.title: Polynomials cannot be all prime
blocks.body: Prove that a nonconstant polynomial $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ cannot take prime values at every positive integer.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $P(n)$ is prime for every $n \ge 1$, and let $p = P(1)$. For every $k \ge 0$, the difference $(1 + kp) - 1 = kp$ divides $P(1 + kp) - P(1)$, so $p \mid P(1 + kp)$. A prime divisible by $p$ equals $p$, so $P(1 + kp) = p$ for all $k \ge 0$.

Then the polynomial $P(x) - p$ has the infinitely many roots $1, 1 + p, 1 + 2p, \dots$, so it is the zero polynomial and $P$ is constant, a contradiction.

For Euler's polynomial, running the same argument from $n = 0$ points straight at a composite value: $41 = P(0)$ divides $P(41) = 41\cdot 43$.

blocks.title: Schur's theorem
blocks.body: Let $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ be nonconstant. Prove that infinitely many primes divide at least one nonzero value $P(n)$ with $n \in \mathbb Z$.
blocks.solution:
If $P(0) = 0$, then $n \mid P(n)$ for every $n$ by the difference divisibility. A nonconstant polynomial has finitely many roots, so $P(p) \ne 0$ for all large primes $p$, and each such $p$ divides $P(p)$.

Now let $c = P(0) \ne 0$ and suppose only the primes $p_1, \dots, p_r$ divide nonzero values of $P$ (allow $r = 0$). Put $M = p_1 p_2\cdots p_r$. Writing $P(x) = c + a_1 x + \dots + a_d x^d$,

$$P(cMx) = c + \sum_{k=1}^{d} a_k c^k M^k x^k = c\,Q(x),\qquad Q(x) = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{d} a_k c^{k-1}M^k x^k.$$

So $Q \in \mathbb Z[x]$, $Q$ is nonconstant (its leading coefficient is $a_d c^{d-1}M^d \ne 0$), and $Q(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i}$ for every $i$ and every integer $x$.

A nonconstant polynomial takes each of the values $0, 1, -1$ only finitely often, so there is an integer $x$ with $|Q(x)| \ge 2$. Let $q$ be a prime factor of $Q(x)$. Then $q$ is none of the $p_i$, since $Q(x) \equiv 1 \pmod{p_i}$. But $q$ divides $c\,Q(x) = P(cMx)$, which is nonzero. This contradicts the assumption.

blocks.body:
- The divisibility $a - b \mid P(a) - P(b)$ needs integer coefficients, not just integer values. The polynomial $P(x) = x(x-1)/2$ takes integer values at all integers, but $2 - 0 = 2$ does not divide $P(2) - P(0) = 1$.
- The rational root theorem only produces candidates; most of them usually fail.
- Lagrange's bound on roots holds modulo a prime $p$, and only when $p$ does not divide the leading coefficient (if $p$ divides every coefficient, every residue is a root). Modulo composites a degree $2$ polynomial can have more than two roots.
- Irreducible over $\mathbb Z$ and over $\mathbb Q$ differ by constants: $2x + 2 = 2(x + 1)$ factors in $\mathbb Z[x]$ but is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. Gauss's lemma is about factorisations into nonconstant factors.

Gauss's lemma and irreducibility criteria are ring theory in $\mathbb Z[x]$; the same argument shows that $\mathbb Z[x]$ has unique factorisation. The basic facts about roots and coefficients are in [[polynomials-roots]].

Prime divisors of values $P(n)$ are where this topic meets algebraic number theory. For the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$, a prime dividing $\Phi_n(m)$ either divides $n$ or is $\equiv 1 \pmod n$ ([[cyclotomic]]); combined with Schur's theorem this proves that there are infinitely many primes $\equiv 1 \pmod n$. In general, for irreducible $P$ and apart from finitely many exceptions, the primes dividing values of $P$ are the primes that have a degree $1$ factor in the ring of integers of a field generated by a root of $P$ ([[ideals]]), and Chebotarev's density theorem gives their density. Divisibility conditions of the form $m - n \mid f(m) - f(n)$ for functions that are not polynomials appear in [[integer-functional-eq]].

1. Show that no $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ satisfies $P(7) = 5$ and $P(15) = 9$.
2. Show that $x^5 + 6x^3 + 3$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.
3. Let $P \in \mathbb Z[x]$ take the value $2$ at three distinct integers. Prove that $P(n) \ne 3$ for every integer $n$.
4. For each prime $p < 50$, decide whether $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$ has a solution, and describe the pattern.
